title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) comparing a deterministic template baseline to a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks scored by a deterministic validator. Under the frozen confirmatory semantics (preregistered shared_initial_candidate per pair), both baseline and guarded conditions passed the verifier on all confirmatory episodes (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). The paired difference is 0.00 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). Artifact traces show this degenerate outcome results from the preregistered shared‑candidate semantics and template‑tight task synthesis (identical canonical candidates were evaluated under both conditions). We publish the exact execution and analysis artifacts (see execution/execution_manifest.json in the bundle) and present artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversification) that preserve reproducibility while enabling informative comparisons about independent generative reliability.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation is an operationally meaningful NetOps problem: generated device commands must preserve reachability, enforce ACL and transient safety invariants, and respect multi‑step change workflows. Deterministic validators that compute configuration semantics (reachability, transient safety, ACL invariants) are standard pre‑deployment tools and provide objective correctness oracles for generated artifacts (see Batfish lessons [https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866]). We preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) to ask: does a single‑pass LLM generation pipeline produce verifier‑valid configurations less often than a deterministic template baseline across programmatic NetOps intent tasks? The preregistration froze task synthesis, scoring rules, generation semantics, seeds, stopping rules, and the deterministic validator before any model outputs were observed.
sections.related_work: Prior work demonstrates that offline, control‑plane and configuration verifiers materially reduce deployment risk by checking semantic invariants prior to deployment; Batfish and related verification systems guided our choice of deterministic validator [https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Recent LLM→NetOps studies have advocated generate‑validate‑repair patterns and highlighted the mismatch between language metrics and operational correctness; many evaluations lack preregistration or exhaustive artifact publication, making it difficult to determine precisely what was tested (e.g., intent‑to‑config pipelines and intent‑based generators in CN S M and network configuration literature [https://doi.org/10.23919/cnsm62983.2024.10814407, https://doi.org/10.1002/nem.70029]). Our work is methodological: a frozen, preregistered paired design with deterministic validator traces and exhaustive SHA‑256 artifact manifests to support byte‑for‑byte reproduction and forensic reanalysis.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study preregistered the primary confirmatory estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the confirmatory analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1. Key preregistered parameters: N = 120 tasks (40 per topology class: edge, datacenter, multi‑AS); confirmatory generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (one canonical candidate generated per pair and evaluated under both conditions); model declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini (see execution/model_configuration.json, SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820); deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) implementing intent constraint checks, transient safety enforcement, and final‑state reachability/ACL checks. The frozen bootstrap plan: 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729, producing percentile CI for the paired difference.

Task generation and templates. Tasks were synthesized from a deterministic template bank (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, version 5.0). Each task manifest entry contains: initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit required_sequence (the minimal safe command sequence), workflow_policies (e.g., make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty annotation (changed_interface_count, transient_rule_count). Representative manifest entries and per‑task JSONs are available in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and in the artifact_examples set (for example: task‑000001 manifest and responses). The templates encode concrete operational safety constraints to give the validator objective, operational semantics.

Generation, adapter and scoring harness. The hosted adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the run used a single shared canonical generation per pair (shared_initial) which was stored as execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt (representative SHA‑256s recorded in the execution manifest). Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation that returns binary VALID_CONFIGURATION when required commands and transient constraints are satisfied. Per‑episode scoring JSONs are archived under execution/scoring/*.json (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json). The complete execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and per‑file SHA‑256 hashes are included in the artifact bundle to permit exact reruns.

Execution accounting and failure policy. Planned_episode_count = 240 (120 pairs × 2 conditions). Completed_episode_count = 240; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 120 (shared_initial generation counted once per pair by the preregistered accounting). The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automatic retries for infrastructure failures; no retries were needed. All provider call traces and call_cache entries (execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/call_cache/*) are published for auditing and exposure analysis.
sections.results:
Confirmatory counts and statistical inference. All confirmatory episodes completed and were scored. Aggregated confirmatory counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv) show baseline_success_count = 120/120 (pass rate 1.00) and guarded_success_count = 120/120 (pass rate 1.00). The paired contingency table is degenerate: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The paired estimator (mean over pairs of guarded_i − baseline_i) = 0.00. Bootstrap inference (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields a 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All analysis artifacts are archived under analysis/ (paired_difference_figure.svg, condition_summary.csv, and paired_contingency_table.csv) for independent verification.

Representative validator traces and identical artifact fingerprints. Archived per‑episode scoring JSONs show full validator traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, final_state, violation_count). For example, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57fff893fe02bd395c435a422f5431376e439875577a8431063) contains the validator's before/after states and reports valid = true and violation_count = 0. The canonical shared candidate for that pair is execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36...). The execution manifest shows that for many pairs the baseline, guarded and shared‑initial response files are byte‑identical (identical SHA‑256s recorded in execution/responses/*), which explains the degenerate contingency counts: identical artifacts evaluated by the same deterministic validator produce identical outcomes.

Deterministic reconciliation and provider accounting. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms accounting consistency: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120; complete_pair_count = 120; n_11 = 120 (all other cells 0). Provider call audits (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/provider_calls/) show 120 completed hosted model call events and no failed hosted calls. These artifacts permit external auditors to reexecute the exact run or to reconfigure generation semantics (for example, re‑running with independent seeds per condition) while preserving determinism for validator scoring.
sections.discussion:
What the confirmatory test measured and what it did not. Artifact traces show the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally removed independent generation variability: one canonical candidate per pair was generated and evaluated under both baseline and guarded conditions. Consequently the confirmatory paired test measured whether the deterministic validator produced different judgments on identical artifacts across conditions (it did not). It therefore cannot be interpreted as evidence about independent LLM generative reliability (the probability that independently sampled LLM candidates satisfy verifier constraints), which is the operational question NetOps teams typically care about.

Artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications to answer independent reliability. Because the entire execution and scoring harness is published with SHA‑256‑indexed artifacts, researchers can immediately reexecute the experiment with modified, preregistered generation semantics to measure independent reliability without fabricating data. Suggested, artifact‑grounded modifications (implementable with the included code and manifests): (1) independent_per_condition confirmatory sampling — generate one independent candidate per condition per pair (baseline_seed_0, guarded_seed_1) and re‑run deterministic_netops_validator_v5 to estimate independent pass probabilities; (2) multi‑seed confirmatory design — generate K ≥ 3 independent seeds per condition per task and estimate per‑condition pass probability with bootstrapped CIs; (3) validator diversification — add a second deterministic verifier (e.g., an alternative reachability analyzer or an emulation harness) and report intersection/union pass rates to reduce validator–task coupling. All code, seeds, task templates and validator harness are published so these reruns are deterministic and reproducible (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl for exact paths and seeds).

Contamination, exposure, and reproducibility caveats. The preregistered contamination heuristics (exact‑match and normalized n‑gram overlap thresholds) recorded no confirmed contamination flags in the confirmatory candidates under the chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not conclusive proof against training‑data exposure. To allow independent exposure audits we publish full provider call traces and call_cache entries (execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/call_cache/*) so reviewers can run alternative exposure heuristics. Reproducibility is preserved by the exhaustive per‑file SHA‑256 manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json), the archived master prompt (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba), and the frozen preregistration SHA noted above.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, verifier‑grounded paired experiment and released a complete artifact bundle enabling byte‑level reproduction. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, both deterministic template baselines and the recorded gpt‑5‑mini guarded pipeline validated on all N = 120 confirmatory tasks (120/120 each), producing a degenerate paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Archived response fingerprints and validator traces explain this outcome: identical canonical candidates were evaluated under both conditions. The artifact record permits immediate, deterministic reruns under alternative, informative generation semantics (independent_per_condition, multi‑seed confirmatory designs, validator diversification) that answer the independent reliability question operators require. All execution and analysis artifacts—including the immutable initial master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and the preregistration SHA—are included in the submission bundle to permit exact audit and corrective reruns. Transparent preregistration plus exhaustive artifact publication clarifies precisely what a confirmatory test measures and accelerates corrective re‑execution that addresses operational questions about LLM generative reliability in NetOps workflows.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produced narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favour canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, reducing independence between conditions and causing the degenerate paired outcome.

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses (seeds_1..4) were not included in the confirmatory inference reported here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates, which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
